children: By Nate Raymond

A federal judge on Wednesday appeared receptive to blocking the Trump administration from barring healthcare providers that receive certain federal HIV-treatment funds from acknowledging their transgender patients' identities or providing them gender-affirming care.

US District Judge William Young during a hearing in Boston questioned the legality of conditions imposed on the grant funding aimed at implementing an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last year prohibiting federal funding for what he calls "gender ideology."
"Where does he get off issuing this?" Young asked, referring to Trump.

The judge said guidelines the US Department of Health and Human Services adopted for the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program in response to Trump's order appeared to interfere with doctor-patient relationships by preventing physicians from using a transgender patient's preferred pronouns, "even as a matter of empathy."

He suggested that the policy may violate the Administrative Procedure Act by imposing an unconstitutional burden on the free speech rights of the plaintiffs, a group of national HIV medical associations and healthcare providers.

Young, an appointee of Republican President Ronald Reagan, pressed a lawyer for the government on how Trump had authority to mandate such restrictions at all, saying the executive order "seems to interfere with matters that are the most private, the most sensitive to the people of the United States: their personhood."

"The order of the president of the United States I think fairly read expresses the view that transgender citizens don't exist," Young told Justice Department attorney Peter Goldstone. "Please tell me I'm wrong."
"I can't," Goldstone responded.
The judge made his comments during a bench trial in a lawsuit that was filed in June by several HIV medical associations and providers, including the American Academy of HIV Medicine.
The
centers on the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program, which Congress created in 1990 to provide medical care for low-income and uninsured people living with HIV.

Beginning in March, the Health Resources and Services Administration, a division of HHS that administers the program, added funding conditions designed to implement Trump's executive order, which had also directed the federal government to recognize only two sexes, male and female.
Under the conditions, providers must ensure funding supports activities using "sex-based definitions grounded in biological reality" and not "social or medical experimentation," the lawsuit said.

"It places providers with a Hobson's choice of giving up necessary funding or giving up their ability to treat their patients in an ethical manner and in a manner that is consistent with ethical standards and even state laws," said Omar Gonzalez-Pagan, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at Lambda Legal.

The plaintiffs contend the policy is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act because it conflicts with the Ryan White Program's statutory mandate to provide comprehensive medical services to HIV patients, which historically has included hormone therapy for transgender individuals.
Goldstone urged Young to reject the case on procedural grounds, arguing that the plaintiffs lack standing as no provider has yet lost funding as a result of the restrictions.
"They still have not yet had that concrete, tangible hardship because those conditions have not yet been triggered," he said.

Young said he would rule "as rapidly as I can" but encouraged settlement discussions. At the parties' request, he agreed to delay a decision until after October 2 to give the administration time to consider the latest settlement proposal from the plaintiffs.
The case is American Academy of HIV Medicine et al v. Health Resources and Services Administration, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, No. 1:26-cv-12638.
For the plaintiffs: Omar Gonzalez-Pagan, Jose Abrigo and Jessica Polansky of Lambda Legal
For the government: Peter Goldstone of the US Department of Justice
